summary: Johannes Hertel was an Indologist who studied at the University of Leipzig under Ernst Windisch (Dr. phil. 1897). He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1920) before holding the chair for Indian philology at Leipzig from 1919 to 1937.

Johannes Klatt was an Indologist who studied at Humboldt University of Berlin under Albrecht Weber and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg under August Friedrich Pott (PhD ~1873). From 1872, he worked at the Royal Library of Berlin, becoming librarian in 1889.

Linguist and philosopher Johannes Lohmann earned his Ph.D. at Humboldt University of Berlin and habilitated under Wilhelm Schulze. He taught at Basel (~1936–1944), held a professorship at Rostock (1940), and was professor of comparative linguistics at Freiburg (1949–1963).
Johannes Mehlig was an Indologist who studied under Friedrich Weller (~1948–1953) and Paul Thieme (~1951–1953).

Working in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, Johannes Nobel studied at Greifswald and Humboldt University of Berlin (PhD under Heinrich Lüders). After teaching at Berlin, he held the chair for Indology at the University of Marburg from 1928 to 1955.

Scholar of Indology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies Johannes Rahder studied at Leiden and Utrecht (Ph.D. under Willem Caland). He was professor at Utrecht (1929–1931), held the chair of Japanese at Leiden (1931–1946), and was professor at Yale (1947–1965).

Johannes Reinoud Abraham Loman was an Indologist who studied at the University of Amsterdam under Adriaan Scharpé and Theodoor Paul Galestin, earning his PhD by 1956. He later held a post at Leiden University from 1958 to 1973.

Linguist and Indologist Johannes Schmidt studied at Bonn, Jena (PhD under August Schleicher), and Berlin. He held chairs for comparative linguistics and Sanskrit at the University of Graz (1873–1876) and Humboldt University of Berlin from 1876.

Johannes Schneider works in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies, having earned a Magister at the University of Marburg. He held posts at FU Berlin, the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and became außerplanmäßiger Professor of Indology at Munich in 2014.

Tibetologist and sinologist Johannes Schubert studied at Leipzig and Humboldt University of Berlin (Ph.D.). He served as a librarian at Leipzig University Library (1928–1954) and taught at the University of Leipzig from 1934, later serving as professor and director.

Johannes Toepffer worked in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Tartu under Leo Meyer and under Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, later holding a post at the University of Basel (~1891–1895).

Scholar of Tibetology and history/archaeology John A. Ardussi completed his PhD at the Australian National University and studied under MA supervisor Turrell V. Wylie. He held research posts at CNRS and served as a Senior Research Fellow at the University of Virginia.

John Alexander Corrie Boswell worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as a colonial civil servant in the Madras Civil Service from 1855 to 1871 and in the Indian Civil Service from around 1856 to 1872.

John Alexander Jorgensen works in Buddhist studies, sinology, and Japanology. He earned his MA at the Australian National University under Kenneth H. J. Gardiner, later holding posts at ANU and as Senior Lecturer at Griffith University.

Linguist John Alexander Stewart studied at the University of Aberdeen (~1899–1903) and served in the Indian Civil Service (~1905–1933). He later held posts as Reader in Burmese at the University of London and at SOAS (~1933–1948).

John Allan, an Indologist and historian, studied at Edinburgh and Leipzig. He served as Deputy Keeper of Coins and Medals at the British Museum (1924–1949) and lectured in Sanskrit at UCL, SOAS, and the University of Edinburgh (1949–1955).

John Anderson, who worked in Indology and archaeology, earned an M.D. at Edinburgh. He was professor of natural history at Free Church College, curator and supervisor at the Indian Museum, Kolkata (1865–1886), and professor of comparative anatomy at Calcutta Medical College.
Indologist John Archibald Boyle studied at Radley College until 1858 and served as a civil servant in the Madras Civil Service beginning in 1865.

Indologist and linguist John Avery studied at Amherst, Yale (under William Dwight Whitney), Berlin, and Tübingen. He served as Professor of Greek at Grinnell College (1870–1877) and Bowdoin College (1877–1887).
John B. Carman is a scholar of Indology and religious studies. He served as director at Harvard University and headed the Center for the Study of World Religions.
